newsitem.title: IRAN: Iranians await Khatami's cabinet of change.
newsitem.headline: Iranians await Khatami's cabinet of change.

text.p: From easing a strict dress code for women to conjuring an economic miracle, many Iranians have high expectations their new president will turn the country around.
But they are aware that Mohammad Khatami, the Islamic republic's fifth president, faces an uphill task to overcome entrenched revolutionaries and influential conservatives.
In 1992 the old guard forced the Shi'ite Moslem clergyman to resign after 10 years as culture minister for failing to crush what they saw as a Western cultural invasion.
Some in Iran now say he could fail in implementing promised economic reforms and relaxing social restrictions.
"Which way will Iran go?" is the question a Western diplomat said Iranians as well as world powers were trying to answer after Khatami's return from obscurity and rise to power.
"Iran today is like a country emerging from a military dictatorship with the strata of that dictatorship still in power," the diplomat added.

Khatami, 54, was elected in May by 20 million out of 29 million votes. He took the oath of office on Monday after being confirmed president on Sunday by supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, whose authority over all institutions of government -- including the presidency -- is paramount.

In a clear sign that he hopes to turn the oil-rich but economically-blighted country around, Khatami hinted in parliament he would try to erase Iran's image publicised by arch-adversary the United States as a rogue state.
And he stressed that the ruling clergy must include ordinary Iranians in the decision-making process.
But removing "Death to America" slogans from the streets of Tehran or changing the name of Khaled al-Islambouli Avenue could take some time.

Egyptian Islamist Islambouli, honoured as a martyr on an Iranian postage stamp, was executed for the 1981 assassination of Egyptian President Anwar al-Sadat, a bitter critic of Iran's 1979 Islamic revolution.

Iranians are waiting to see the shape of Khatami's cabinet which he must present for parliamentary approval by August 18. Previous presidents submitted their lists of ministers shortly after being sworn in.
But Khatami, a middle-ranking cleric who is a tolerant, moderate politician in the Iranian context, is apparently reviewing some of the candidates who analysts said risked rejection by the assembly.

"It is very difficult to balance all these forces," said a diplomat. Hardline conservatives, liberal mullahs and voters including professionals, youth and women who gave Khatami his victory are all vying for influence.
While the country waits to see who will be in and who will be out, ministers appointed by Khatami's predecessor Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani remain in office.

Khatami "will make only little change but even if he wants to make (drastic social changes) he cannot," said Shereen, an applied chemistry student who dreams of the day the Islamic dress code which requires women to conceal their curves and cover their hair would be relaxed.
"You know why," she added when asked about her prediction.
A mullah passing in front of a Tehran cinema where artists gathered to celebrate Khatami's rise to power calmly commented that he did not expect Khatami to shake up the country.
"No. We all obey Islam and Khatami is a clergyman who is committed to Islam," said the mullah.

Economists and businessmen hope Khatami will improve Iran's relations with the West to encourage the transfer of foreign capital needed to jump-start an economy plagued with high inflation and unemployment.
On the home front they say Khatami has to cut the number of government employees and open the economy to the private sector.

"As long as the Iranian banking, industrial... the entire economy is centralised and the government is doing the private sector's job, I do not think the economy will pick up," said Amir Amini, senior adviser at the Iran Chamber of Commerce.
